a: in the second jubilee of years
p: The Ge'ez says "in the two jubilee," which cannot fit the book's dates. Charles emended the reading of all his manuscripts to "twenty-seventh."

readings.en: in the two jubilee of years (a cardinal number)
readings.plain: in the second jubilee of years

readings.w: Charles's manuscripts, as cited in Charles 1902 ("the reading of all the MSS"; the Source Library copy of the note gives it as "twenty-second jubilee")
readings.en: in the twenty-second jubilee of years
readings.plain: in the twenty-second jubilee of years

readings.en: in the twenty-seventh jubilee of years
readings.plain: in the twenty-seventh jubilee of years

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's Ge'ez, the base text, and does not correct it silently, though it gives the cardinal "two" as "second." The reading cannot be right: Noah was born in the fifteenth jubilee (4:28). VanderKam's "two" may be what is left of "twenty-two," the number Charles's note gives for his manuscripts. Charles emended to "twenty-seventh" (his printed Ge'ez text has "twenty-sixth," by a slip, he says), which gives the year 1307 from creation, the total the Samaritan Chronicle gives "from Adam to the Flood." The date 1307 rests on that emendation. The EOTC printed Bible (digital copy) has the same words as VanderKam here; it follows VanderKam's text so closely in these chapters that it is not a second witness.

a: He appeared on the earth.
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez says Noah "appeared" on the earth. Charles's text says he "made atonement for the earth."

readings.en: and he appeared on the earth
readings.plain: He appeared on the earth.

readings.en: and he made atonement for the earth
readings.plain: He made atonement for the earth.

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam. The verb ʾästärʾäyä means "appear, be seen," as in 5:30 ("the tops of the mountains could be seen"). Charles's English has "made atonement," which would be ʾästäsräyä, the verb used later in the same verse; the two words share most of their letters but differ in two. Charles's 1902 English prints "made atonement" twice, and his note says Jewish haggadah "knows nothing of this particular act of atonement." Charles's reading fits the verse well, but the base text is not obviously wrong: Noah steps out and is seen on the dry earth. The EOTC printed Bible (digital copy) has the same words here; it follows VanderKam's text so closely in these chapters that it is not a second witness.

a: from the hand of every one
p: The Ge'ez says "from the hand of every one." Charles added "beast," from Genesis 9:5.

readings.en: from the hand of all (every one)
readings.plain: from the hand of every one

readings.en: at the hand of every (beast)
readings.plain: from the hand of every beast

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam. Charles supplied ʾənsəsa, "beast," which he thought had dropped out before the next word, so that the verse would match Genesis 9:5 ("From every animal I will demand it"). The Ge'ez makes sense as it stands. The EOTC printed Bible (digital copy) has the same words here; it follows VanderKam's text so closely in these chapters that it is not a second witness.

a: pleading for themselves
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez: the priests plead "for them." Charles's English: "on your behalf." Goes with the next entry.

readings.en: pleading on their behalf
readings.plain: pleading for themselves

readings.en: supplicating on your behalf
readings.plain: pleading on your behalf

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam, whose Ge'ez has bäʾnətiʾähomu, "for them," in both places of this verse. Charles's English has "on your behalf" in both. The meaning hardly changes: Israel's offerings plead for Israel. The EOTC printed Bible (digital copy) has the same words here; it follows VanderKam's text so closely in these chapters that it is not a second witness.

a: seek forgiveness for themselves
p: The second "for them" of this verse. Goes with the entry before.

readings.en: they ask pardon on their behalf
readings.plain: seek forgiveness for themselves

readings.en: they shall seek forgiveness on your behalf
readings.plain: seek forgiveness on your behalf

why: See the entry on "pleading for themselves." Charles notes on this phrase that he kept the reading of his manuscripts. The EOTC printed Bible (digital copy) has the same words here; it follows VanderKam's text so closely in these chapters that it is not a second witness.

a: But Abraham alone kept it
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez says "Abraham alone." Charles printed "But Abraham," with his manuscript a.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's manuscripts b, c, d (as cited in Charles 1902)
readings.en: and Abraham alone kept (it)
readings.plain: But Abraham alone kept it

readings.en: but Abraham observed it
readings.plain: But Abraham kept it

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam, whose text agrees with three of Charles's four manuscripts. "Alone" sharpens the point that Abraham kept the feast when no one else did.

a: until I renewed it for them
p: VanderKam: "until I renewed it for them." Charles's text: "until you celebrated it anew."

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's manuscripts b, c, d (as cited in Charles 1902)
readings.en: until I renewed it for them
readings.plain: until I renewed it for them

readings.en: until ye celebrated it anew
readings.plain: until you held it anew

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam (ḥädäskəwomu, "I renewed it for them"). Charles's note gives both forms: manuscript a has "you (plural) renewed," the others "I renewed." In VanderKam's reading the speaker, God or the angel, renews the feast at Sinai; in Charles's, Israel does.

a: Aram and Lud
t: Aram and Lud, or Aram, children?
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez ends "Aram wəlud." Charles emended and printed Lud before Aram.

readings.en: Aram (and) Lud, or: Aram, children
readings.plain: Aram and Lud

readings.en: and Lud, and Aram
readings.plain: Lud and Aram

why: The Plain English Translation reads VanderKam's wəlud as "and Lud," since Genesis 10:22 lists Lud among Shem's sons; the same letters can also mean "children." Charles emended the verse and put Lud before Aram, the order of Genesis 10:22. Neither reading changes who Shem's sons are.

a: Yarbeh
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez has yarbəḥ. Charles's English has "the Giants."

readings.en: and yarbəḥ killed the Naphil
readings.plain: Yarbeh

readings.en: and the Giants slew the Naphil
readings.plain: the giants

why: The Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam's word as a name, since no meaning for it can be checked. Charles's "the Giants" gives the three kinds of giants of the Greek of 1 Enoch 7 that he cites in his note (great giants, the Nephilim, the Eliud); with VanderKam's word the sentence names four. Charles's note does not say what Ge'ez lies behind his "Giants."

a: After these came all the others
p: The Ge'ez has no verb here. Charles supplied "they sinned against" from 1 Enoch 7:5.

readings.en: and after these, all of them
readings.plain: After these came all the others

readings.en: and after this they sinned against the beasts and birds
readings.plain: After this they sinned against the wild animals and the birds

why: The Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam's Ge'ez and supplies only "came." Charles added "they sinned against" from 1 Enoch 7:5. With his words the animals are victims; without them they join in the bloodshed, as in 5:2.

a: who made heaven and earth
p: Charles's English adds "and all things" after "heaven and earth." VanderKam's Ge'ez does not have it.

readings.en: creator of heaven and earth
readings.plain: who made heaven and earth

readings.en: who created heaven and earth and all things
readings.plain: who made heaven and earth and all things

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam. Charles's extra words do not change the sense.

a: daughter of Abaday son of Japheth
p: The Ge'ez has "Abaday." Charles emended it to "Madai," with the Syriac list and a Greek manuscript.

readings.orig: ወለተ አበዳይ ወልደ ያፌት (wälätä ʾäbäday wäldä yafet)
readings.en: daughter of Abaday, son of Japheth
readings.plain: daughter of Abaday son of Japheth

readings.w: Charles's emended text, with the Syriac list of wives and Lagarde's Greek manuscript r (as Charles reports)
readings.en: daughter of Madai, son of Japheth
readings.plain: daughter of Madai son of Japheth

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam. Charles's correction is attractive, since Japheth has a son Madai (7:19; Genesis 10:2) and no son Abaday, and the two names differ by little in Ge'ez. In either reading Kainam marries into Japheth's family.

a: in the thirtieth jubilee
p: The Ge'ez has a stray "in the year" before "in the thirtieth jubilee." Charles reads "the one and thirtieth."

readings.en: in the year, and in the thirtieth jubilee
readings.plain: in the thirtieth jubilee

readings.en: in the one and thirtieth jubilee
readings.plain: in the thirty-first jubilee

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's number but leaves the stray word bäʿamät, "in the year," untranslated, since it makes no sense before "and in the thirtieth jubilee." Charles's English reads "one and thirtieth," which fits the dates better: Shelah was born in the thirtieth jubilee (8:5) and his son Eber is born before the thirty-second (8:7).

a: In the fourth year he was born.
p: Charles brackets "And in the fourth year he was born" as a dittography from 8:5.

readings.en: and in the fourth year he was born
readings.plain: In the fourth year he was born.

readings.w: Charles's text (1902), the clause in brackets
readings.en: [And in the fourth year he was born]
readings.plain: (the clause left out)

why: The Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam's text. Charles's note calls the bracketed words "a dittography from preceding verse": 8:5 has already said that Shelah was born in the fourth year. Read as it stands, the clause repeats the date of Shelah's birth before his marriage.

a: in a wicked way
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez says the first division was made "in evil." Charles's English has "secretly."

readings.en: in evil, wickedly
readings.plain: in a wicked way

readings.en: secretly
readings.plain: secretly

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam (bäʾəkuy, "in evil"). Charles's 1902 note on the word points back to his note on 4:5 without giving the Ge'ez. Either way the first division was not the lawful one that follows in 8:10-11.

a: on the south side of it, to the south
p: Charles brackets the second "to the south" as a dittography and says "south" is better translated "north."

readings.en: toward its south, to the south
readings.plain: on the south side of it, to the south

readings.en: to the south thereof, [to the south]
readings.plain: on the south side of it

why: The Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam's Ge'ez. Charles's note brackets the repeated phrase as copied twice by mistake, and on "south" here says, "Better translate 'north.'" In his note on 10:28 he explains that the word rendered "south" rightly means "north" but is sometimes used the other way by Ethiopic scribes. The Plain English Translation keeps the sense Charles's English gives throughout chapters 8-10.

a: The first portion came out for Elam and his sons
p: VanderKam: the first portion of Shem's land is Elam's. Charles's English has "Ham."

readings.en: for Elam
readings.plain: The first portion came out for Elam and his sons

readings.en: for Ham and his sons
readings.plain: The first portion came out for Ham and his sons

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam. Shem is dividing his own land, and Elam is his first son (7:18; Genesis 10:22). Charles's own note on this verse explains Elam as "the name of Shem's eldest son," so the "Ham" of his English looks like a slip.

a: it goes up to the Wadafa River
p: Charles calls wadafâ falag untranslatable and emended it to "and skirts the river."

readings.en: and it goes up, wädäfa river
readings.plain: it goes up to the Wadafa River

readings.en: and it ascends and skirts the river
readings.plain: it goes up and runs along the river

why: The Plain English Translation reads wädäfa as a river's name, the reading Charles allows "if wadafâ were the name of a river," and supplies "to." Charles found the words "untranslateable" as they stand in his manuscripts a, b, d and emended them to wawadafa falaga, "and skirts the river." No river of this name appears elsewhere in the book.

a: over the children of your children
p: VanderKam: "the children of your children." Charles printed "my sons," with manuscript a.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's manuscript b reads "thy sons' sons" (as cited in Charles 1902)
readings.en: the children of your children
readings.plain: over the children of your children

readings.en: my sons
readings.plain: over my sons

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam. Noah's calling his descendants God's "children's children" is the harder reading, and a copyist is more likely to have changed it to the plain "my sons" than the other way round.

a: for you alone know their judgment
t: Know their judgment, or rule over them?
p: VanderKam: "you alone know their judgment." Charles emended to "you alone can exercise dominion over them."

readings.orig: አንተ ባሕቲትከ ታአምር ኵነኔሆሙ (ʾäntä baḥtitkä taʾämr kʷənänehomu)
readings.en: for you alone know their judgment
readings.plain: for you alone know their judgment

readings.en: for Thou alone canst exercise dominion over them
readings.plain: for you alone can rule over them

why: The Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam's Ge'ez, which makes sense: Noah appeals to God as the only one who knows how the spirits are to be judged. Charles changed one word to fit the request that they not rule.

a: to serve before Satan on the earth
p: The Ge'ez verb can mean "be subject, serve" or "carry out judgment."

readings.orig: ከመ ይኰንኑ ቅድመ ሰይጣን ዲበ ምድር (kämä yəkʷännu qədmä säyṭan dibä mədr)
readings.en: so that they may be subject before Satan on the earth
readings.plain: to serve before Satan on the earth

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989), read as "judge" (the sense of the Hebrew Book of Noah's parallel, as Charles quotes it)
readings.en: so that they may carry out judgment before Satan on the earth
readings.plain: to carry out judgment before Satan on the earth

why: This is one text read two ways, not two texts. The Plain English Translation takes the verb as "serve," with Charles's English ("might be subject before Satan"). The other sense fits Charles's quotation from the Hebrew Book of Noah, where the tenth go "before the prince of the Mastema, to rule over the godless, to smite them and to plague them."

a: and ten stades
p: The Ge'ez says "ten stades." A Greek quotation and Charles's text say thirteen.

readings.en: and ten stades
readings.plain: and ten stades

readings.w: Greek quotation in the Catena of Nicephorus (as cited in Charles 1902); Charles's English (1913)
readings.en: the length of one wall was thirteen stades
readings.plain: and thirteen stades

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam. The Greek, which is older than the Ge'ez, gives thirteen stades for one wall and a height of 8,000 cubits, where the Ge'ez has 5,433. Charles kept 5,433 but took thirteen from the Greek. The numbers in this verse were clearly damaged in copying, and no reading of them is certain.
b: A stade (Greek stadion) was about 600 feet, the length of a racecourse.

a: from the border of Lebanon
p: VanderKam: "from the border of Lebanon." Charles printed "Jordan," with his manuscripts a and d.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's manuscripts b, c (as cited in Charles 1902)
readings.en: from the side of Lebanon
readings.plain: from the border of Lebanon

readings.en: from the border of Jordan
readings.plain: from the border of the Jordan

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam. "Jordan" gives a clearer eastern limit, but "Lebanon" repeats the land just named, which a copyist may have changed to Jordan to make the borders plain.

a: from Elam, Asshur and Arpachshad
p: VanderKam: Madai begged land "from Elam, Asshur and Arpachshad." Charles's English has "Ham" for Elam.

readings.orig: እምኀበ ኤላም ወአሱር ወአርፋክስድ (ʾəmḫäbä ʾelam wäʾäsur wäʾärfaksəd)
readings.en: from Elam and Asshur and Arpachshad
readings.plain: from Elam, Asshur and Arpachshad

readings.en: from Ham and Asshur and Arpachshad
readings.plain: from Ham, Asshur and Arpachshad

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam. Elam, Asshur and Arpachshad are all sons of Shem, so they can be "his wife's brothers" if Madai married a daughter of Shem (7:18). "Ham" fits poorly, since Ham is Madai's uncle and settled in the south (10:28).
